Outcomes of stopping: with slow tapering about two-thirds of patients stop completely; in a 10-year Dutch follow-up, 60% of people who stopped after a GP's letter remained abstinent; a meta-analysis of 24 intervention studies found routine care less effective than gradual dose reduction alone or combined with psychological techniques or drug substitution. Elderly people have a worse prognosis. [Source: 'gradual dose reduction' and 'pharmacological substitutions', p. 2094.]

Flumazenil can precipitate withdrawal (shown in a controlled study of people on long-term low doses); a series of studies found flumazenil treatment more effective than tapering or placebo, but it involves in-patient treatment, is likely to suit only a small number of severely dependent people, and large randomized trials had not been done. [The source does not call the studies small.]

The author writes that withdrawal in pregnancy should never be abrupt (citing ref. 174) and that continued use into late pregnancy may cause a neonatal withdrawal syndrome in the baby that can be severe. [Attributed, so it does not read as the encyclopedia's advice.]

In high-dose misuse, as with low-dose dependence, tolerance sets in rapidly and attempted stopping can bring withdrawal that is sometimes severe, with fits and psychotic reactions; high-dose use with opiates is implicated in potentially fatal overdoses; mortality seems to be increased among people who misuse benzodiazepines, though data are sparse.
